questions.question: An adult states the date and location correctly but cannot explain the consequences of refusing care. What should the EMT do next?

choices.text: Assess understanding and judgment further; consult medical direction if capacity remains uncertain
Accept refusal because the patient is oriented
Ask the accompanying relative to make the decision
Use a signed refusal form to resolve the capacity concern

questions.explanation: Orientation is one finding; decision-making capacity also requires understanding and using relevant information.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Orientation alone does not establish capacity for this decision.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A relative’s presence does not automatically authorize substitute decisions.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A signature cannot substitute for capacity assessment.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Orientation is one finding; decision-making capacity also requires understanding and using relevant information.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Orientation alone does not establish capacity for this decision.
questions.keyDistinction: Orientation is one finding; decision-making capacity also requires understanding and using relevant information.

questions.question: An unconscious adult has a life-threatening condition. No authorized decision maker or applicable treatment-limiting order is available. What supports starting necessary emergency care?

choices.text: Implied consent under the emergency doctrine
Expressed consent inferred from the absence of a refusal
Involuntary consent based solely on unconsciousness
Consent that must first be obtained from a relative

questions.explanation: The emergency doctrine permits necessary care when the patient cannot decide and timely consent is unavailable.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Absence of refusal is not an affirmative expression of consent.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Involuntary care involves distinct legal authority; this is emergency implied consent.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Searching for a relative should not delay immediately necessary care.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: The emergency doctrine permits necessary care when the patient cannot decide and timely consent is unavailable.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Absence of refusal is not an affirmative expression of consent.
questions.keyDistinction: The emergency doctrine permits necessary care when the patient cannot decide and timely consent is unavailable.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Consent · Emergency implied consent

questions.question: After an EMT explains a blood pressure measurement, a capable patient nods and extends an arm. How should this consent be classified?

choices.text: Expressed consent communicated nonverbally
Implied consent because the patient did not speak
Involuntary consent because the EMT initiated the request
Substitute consent because the EMT explained the procedure

questions.explanation: A clear informed action can express consent; expressed consent need not be spoken.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Implied consent is not the category for an affirmative nonverbal agreement.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Initiating an explanation does not make voluntary agreement involuntary.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Substitute consent comes from an authorized decision maker, not the clinician.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: A clear informed action can express consent; expressed consent need not be spoken.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Consent · Nonverbal expressed consent

questions.question: Which situation describes an emancipated minor rather than another basis for providing care to a minor?

choices.text: A minor legally treated as an adult for consent under applicable law
A teacher acting in place of an unavailable parent
A child receiving immediately necessary care when a parent cannot be reached
A parent authorizing treatment for a child from another location

questions.explanation: Emancipation concerns the minor’s legal status; emergency doctrine and substitute authority are different routes to consent.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: This concerns in loco parentis, not emancipation.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Emergency care does not itself change the child’s legal status.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Parental authorization is not the minor’s independent adult status.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Emancipation concerns the minor’s legal status; emergency doctrine and substitute authority are different routes to consent.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Consent · Emancipated minor

questions.question: A child has a life-threatening injury. A parent cannot be reached promptly and no authorized decision maker is present. Which approach best fits the consent requirement?

choices.text: Provide immediately necessary care under implied consent
Delay care while dispatch continues trying to reach a parent
Ask an adult bystander to authorize care as a substitute parent
Treat the child’s agreement as adult consent regardless of legal status

questions.explanation: Necessary emergency care can proceed under implied consent when timely authorization is unavailable.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Continuing contact attempts is useful but should not delay necessary emergency care.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: An unrelated bystander does not automatically have parental authority.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Agreement alone does not establish adult legal consent status.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Necessary emergency care can proceed under implied consent when timely authorization is unavailable.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Continuing contact attempts is useful but should not delay necessary emergency care.
questions.keyDistinction: Necessary emergency care can proceed under implied consent when timely authorization is unavailable.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Consent · Minor emergency

questions.question: A restrained patient becomes cyanotic and struggles to breathe. Scene safety can be maintained while the crew reassesses. What should take priority?

choices.text: Address airway and breathing and correct the restraint-related hazard
Check restraint security before changing the position
Begin rapid transport and defer restraint changes until arrival
Wait for medical control to authorize reassessment

questions.explanation: A new breathing compromise requires immediate assessment and correction of a potentially lethal restraint hazard.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Security matters, but maintaining a restraint that compromises breathing is unsafe.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Transport does not replace correcting an immediate breathing hazard.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Urgent reassessment should not await permission; follow applicable restraint and airway protocols.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: A new breathing compromise requires immediate assessment and correction of a potentially lethal restraint hazard.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Security matters, but maintaining a restraint that compromises breathing is unsafe.
questions.keyDistinction: A new breathing compromise requires immediate assessment and correction of a potentially lethal restraint hazard.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Consent · Restraint safety

questions.question: A patient offers to sign a refusal form before the EMT explains the suspected problem and risks. What is the best next step?

choices.text: Explain concerns and alternatives and assess understanding
Obtain a witness signature before discussing risks
Complete the form using the patient’s stated refusal as evidence of capacity
Ask medical control to authorize discharge without further patient discussion

questions.explanation: The refusal process must establish informed decision making; the form documents that process.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: A witness signature does not establish that the refusal was informed.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A statement or signature alone does not establish understanding.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Medical consultation supports the process rather than replacing communication with the patient.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: The refusal process must establish informed decision making; the form documents that process.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: A witness signature does not establish that the refusal was informed.
questions.keyDistinction: The refusal process must establish informed decision making; the form documents that process.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: The Right to Refuse Treatment · Refusal before signature

questions.question: A capable adult continues to refuse after assessment, risk counseling, and indicated medical consultation. Which remaining plan best completes the refusal process?

choices.text: Reoffer care, give follow-up and return advice, seek signatures, and document findings and discussions
Obtain signatures and record the patient’s refusal without the assessment findings
Give return advice and omit the record because medical control was consulted
Document the assessment and leave without explaining when to seek help

questions.explanation: A completed refusal includes continued encouragement, safety advice, requested signatures, and a record of the full process.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Signatures alone do not document assessment, capacity, and counseling.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Consultation does not replace the patient-care record.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Documentation does not replace needed follow-up and return advice.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: A completed refusal includes continued encouragement, safety advice, requested signatures, and a record of the full process.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: The Right to Refuse Treatment · Completed informed refusal

questions.question: An EMT removes a patient’s name from a proposed social-media post. The unusual injury, location, and photograph still identify the patient. No disclosure is authorized. What is the best decision?

choices.text: Do not post the patient-identifying information
Post because the direct identifier has been removed
Post only to a private group of EMS coworkers
Post if a bystander has already shared footage

questions.explanation: Removing a name does not make otherwise identifiable health information appropriate for unauthorized disclosure.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Other details can still identify the patient.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Group membership does not automatically create an authorized care-related purpose.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Someone else’s disclosure does not authorize the EMT’s disclosure.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Removing a name does not make otherwise identifiable health information appropriate for unauthorized disclosure.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Other details can still identify the patient.
questions.keyDistinction: Removing a name does not make otherwise identifiable health information appropriate for unauthorized disclosure.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Confidentiality · Social media privacy

questions.question: A relative requests an identifiable patient-care report. No patient release or other authorized disclosure basis has been established. What should the EMT do?

choices.text: Use the agency’s confidentiality process before releasing protected information
Release the report because being related to the patient is sufficient authorization
Release it if the relative promises not to share it
Remove only the patient’s name and release the otherwise identifiable report

questions.explanation: Patient-care information is confidential. A request or a promise does not establish authorization; follow the agency’s release process.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Relationship alone does not establish an authorized release.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A promise about future use does not authorize disclosure.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Other identifying information remains protected.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: A non-court-order subpoena requires verification of applicable privacy conditions; it is neither automatic permission nor an automatic prohibition.
questions.whyTempting: A relative may have genuine concerns, but the request does not establish a disclosure basis.
questions.whyNotBest: Relationship alone does not establish an authorized release.
questions.keyDistinction: Patient-care information is confidential. A request or a promise does not establish authorization; follow the agency’s release process.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Confidentiality · Subpoena handling

questions.question: A patient with a valid DNR order has a pulse, is breathing, and reports discomfort. No other treatment limitation is identified. Which plan best respects the order?

choices.text: Provide indicated supportive and comfort care under applicable protocols
Limit care to transport because DNR prohibits active treatment
Withhold oxygen and symptom relief until the patient revokes the DNR
Provide usual care but disregard the DNR if arrest occurs

questions.explanation: A DNR limits resuscitation; it does not by itself prohibit indicated supportive care.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: DNR alone does not restrict care to transportation.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Supportive care does not generally require revoking a DNR.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: The applicable resuscitation limitation still matters if arrest occurs.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: A DNR limits resuscitation; it does not by itself prohibit indicated supportive care.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: DNR alone does not restrict care to transportation.
questions.keyDistinction: A DNR limits resuscitation; it does not by itself prohibit indicated supportive care.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Advance Directives · DNR supportive care

questions.question: A family asks EMS to withhold resuscitation. The available document’s applicability cannot be established. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Follow the applicable resuscitation protocol while seeking prompt medical-control clarification
Accept the family’s interpretation as equivalent to a verified EMS order
Withhold care until the document’s status is resolved
Disregard the document because the crew cannot immediately interpret it

questions.explanation: Uncertainty requires the EMS verification process and prompt medical direction without an unsupported delay in indicated care.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Family information matters but does not automatically establish an applicable medical order.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Unverified limitations should not create an unsupported delay in indicated care.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: An unclear document merits clarification rather than dismissal.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Uncertainty requires the EMS verification process and prompt medical direction without an unsupported delay in indicated care.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Family information matters but does not automatically establish an applicable medical order.
questions.keyDistinction: Uncertainty requires the EMS verification process and prompt medical direction without an unsupported delay in indicated care.

reviewReferences.label: Chapter 3 outline
reviewReferences.section: Advance Directives · Advance directive uncertainty

questions.question: A patient is unresponsive, apneic, and pulseless. No applicable DNR or obvious irreversible-death finding is identified. Why do these findings not by themselves justify withholding resuscitation?

choices.text: They establish arrest but do not establish irreversible death
They establish irreversible death once all three occur together
They justify withholding unless a relative requests CPR
They justify withholding once the skin feels cool

questions.explanation: Absent pulse and breathing are arrest findings; withholding requires the applicable protocol’s criteria.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: The combination can occur in potentially resuscitable arrest.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: A relative’s request is not what distinguishes arrest from irreversible death.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Cool skin alone is not conclusive evidence of irreversible death.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Absent pulse and breathing are arrest findings; withholding requires the applicable protocol’s criteria.

reviewReferences.section: Physical Signs of Death · Presumptive versus definitive

questions.question: Postmortem discoloration appears in the lowest body regions because blood settles with gravity. Which term describes this finding?

choices.text: Dependent lividity
Rigor mortis
Algor mortis
Putrefaction

questions.explanation: Dependent lividity describes gravitational blood settling and resulting dependent discoloration.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Rigor mortis is postmortem muscle stiffening.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Algor mortis is postmortem cooling.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Putrefaction is decomposition.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Dependent lividity describes gravitational blood settling and resulting dependent discoloration.

reviewReferences.section: Physical Signs of Death · Dependent lividity

questions.question: An injured patient carries an organ-donor card and needs immediate treatment. How should donor status affect the initial priority?

choices.text: Provide lifesaving care first and communicate donor information as appropriate
Confirm donation eligibility before beginning treatment
Prioritize transport to a transplant center over the patient’s immediate clinical needs
Use the card as authority to limit resuscitation

questions.explanation: The donor’s own life remains the priority; donor status can be communicated without delaying care.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Donation verification should not delay lifesaving treatment.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Destination decisions must serve current clinical needs under applicable protocols.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: A donor designation is not a DNR.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: The donor’s own life remains the priority; donor status can be communicated without delaying care.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: Donation verification should not delay lifesaving treatment.
questions.keyDistinction: The donor’s own life remains the priority; donor status can be communicated without delaying care.

reviewReferences.section: Special Situations · Organ donor priority

questions.question: An altered patient wears a bracelet listing a medical condition and an emergency contact. What is the best use of this information?

choices.text: Use it to guide assessment while continuing care for current threats
Accept the listed condition as the diagnosis and omit other assessment
Complete contact verification before treating immediate threats
Disregard the bracelet until the patient can confirm its accuracy

questions.explanation: Medical identification supplies useful clues but complements current assessment and urgent care.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: A history clue does not exclude other causes or threats.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Contact verification should not delay necessary treatment.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Information can assist assessment even if the patient cannot confirm it.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Medical identification supplies useful clues but complements current assessment and urgent care.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: A history clue does not exclude other causes or threats.
questions.keyDistinction: Medical identification supplies useful clues but complements current assessment and urgent care.

reviewReferences.section: Special Situations · Medical ID during assessment

questions.question: An EMT may perform a procedure under state rules but performs it less carefully than a reasonably competent EMT would. Which distinction applies?

choices.text: Scope concerns authorization; standard of care concerns expected performance
Scope concerns expected performance; standard of care concerns authorization
State authorization means the standard of care is met whenever the procedure is attempted
A poor outcome alone proves the procedure exceeded scope

questions.explanation: Permission to perform a skill and the expected manner of performing it are separate questions.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: This reverses the two concepts.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Authorization does not excuse deficient performance.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: An outcome alone does not determine whether a skill was authorized.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Permission to perform a skill and the expected manner of performing it are separate questions.

questions.question: An off-duty EMT voluntarily begins patient care. A replacement clinician has not yet accepted responsibility. What follows from beginning care?

choices.text: The EMT must continue appropriate care until an accepted transfer or another lawful end of care
The EMT may leave because there was no initial duty to respond
The patient’s location at an emergency facility ends the EMT’s responsibility automatically
The duty applies only if the EMT is paid for the encounter

questions.explanation: Beginning care creates a responsibility to follow through appropriately, even when the initial assistance was voluntary.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: The original off-duty status does not remove responsibility after beginning care.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Physical arrival is not automatically an accepted handoff.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Payment is not what creates this follow-through responsibility.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Beginning care creates a responsibility to follow through appropriately, even when the initial assistance was voluntary.

questions.question: Which combination contains the four elements required to establish negligence?

choices.text: Duty, breach of duty, damages, and causation
Duty, breach of duty, damages, and intent to harm
Duty, breach of duty, consent, and causation
Duty, foreseeable risk, damages, and certification

questions.explanation: Negligence requires a duty, a breach, actual damages, and a causal connection between the breach and damages.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Intent to harm is not a required negligence element; causation is missing.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Consent does not replace damages.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Foreseeable risk and certification do not replace breach and causation.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Negligence requires a duty, a breach, actual damages, and a causal connection between the breach and damages.

questions.question: A capable adult expressly refuses a nonemergency procedure. No emergency exception or other legal authority applies. The EMT performs it anyway. Which term most directly describes the unauthorized physical contact?

choices.text: Battery
Assault
False imprisonment
Abandonment

questions.explanation: Battery concerns unauthorized or unlawful physical contact.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: Assault concerns creating apprehension of harmful contact; the defining fact here is actual contact.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: False imprisonment concerns unlawful restriction of movement.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Abandonment concerns improperly ending an established care relationship.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Battery concerns unauthorized or unlawful physical contact.

questions.question: A crew arrives at the ED, but no appropriate clinician has accepted responsibility for the patient. What should the crew do?

choices.text: Continue care and arrange an accepted clinical handoff
Leave after delivering a written report to the nursing desk
End care once the patient is inside the receiving facility
Treat an administrative arrival signature as acceptance of clinical responsibility

questions.explanation: Physical arrival or paperwork does not by itself complete the transfer of patient care.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: A report left at a desk does not establish that a clinician accepted care.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Location alone does not complete the handoff.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: An administrative signature does not necessarily establish clinical acceptance.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: Physical arrival or paperwork does not by itself complete the transfer of patient care.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: A report left at a desk does not establish that a clinician accepted care.
questions.keyDistinction: Physical arrival or paperwork does not by itself complete the transfer of patient care.

questions.question: Findings raise concern for child abuse during a call. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Treat current needs, record objective findings, and report through the required process
Delay reporting until the EMT can establish who caused the injuries
Document the concern but rely on another agency to decide whether reporting is needed
Promise confidentiality to encourage disclosure and report only with the family’s permission

questions.explanation: The EMT provides care, documents facts, and follows applicable mandated-reporting requirements rather than trying to prove the case.

incorrectChoiceExplanations.B: The EMT is not required to establish the perpetrator before following the reporting process.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.C: Documentation does not replace an applicable reporting duty.
incorrectChoiceExplanations.D: Mandatory reporting cannot be conditioned on a promise of secrecy or family approval.

questions.yieldBasis: Inferred study priority, not an official exam blueprint
questions.diagnosticIntent: The EMT provides care, documents facts, and follows applicable mandated-reporting requirements rather than trying to prove the case.
questions.whyTempting: This alternative addresses part of the situation.
questions.whyNotBest: The EMT is not required to establish the perpetrator before following the reporting process.
questions.keyDistinction: The EMT provides care, documents facts, and follows applicable mandated-reporting requirements rather than trying to prove the case.

questions.question: A capable patient understands the recommended care but declines it for personal religious reasons. The EMT believes the treatment would help. Which response best reflects professional ethics?

choices.text: Respect the informed choice while explaining options and offering appropriate care
Treat disagreement with the recommendation as proof of impaired capacity
Let the accompanying family override the patient’s informed choice
Continue persuasion until agreement is obtained before recognizing refusal
